question: Ece texts, “I’m running late for lunch.” What does she mean?
choices: She’ll get there after the time you agreed.
She has to leave lunch earlier than planned.
She can only stay for a few minutes today.
She’s already there and waiting for you.
note: If you’re running late, you’ll arrive after the time you agreed. It says nothing about leaving early. For that, Ece might text, “I’ll have to leave early.”

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: You invite Ali to play football on Saturday. He replies, “Count me in!” What does he mean?
choices: He’d like to play with you on Saturday.
He wants you to keep the score for him.
He needs a few days before he decides.
He’ll come and watch, but he won’t play.
note: “Count me in!” is an informal yes: add me to the group. If Ali couldn’t play, he might say, “Count me out this time.”

question: Your study group meets at four. Jo asks, “Can we bring it forward an hour?” What time does she want to meet?
choices: Three o’clock.
Four o’clock.
Five o’clock.
Six o’clock.
note: Bringing a meeting forward moves it to an earlier time. To move it an hour later, Jo would ask, “Can we put it back an hour?”

question: Your cousin says, “I’ll pick you up on my way to the match.” What is she offering?
choices: To stop for you and take you with her.
To save you a seat at the match.
To buy your ticket at the gate on her way.
To meet you outside the stadium afterwards.
note: To pick someone up is to collect them, usually by car, and travel on together. If she only wanted to meet you there, she’d say, “See you at the match.”

question: You ask whether to travel on Friday or Saturday. Your friend says, “Let’s leave it open for now.” What does he mean?
choices: You’ll pick the day when you know more.
You’ll travel on both of the days.
He wants to call off the trip completely.
He’d like to book the Friday trip today.
note: Leaving a plan open means deciding later, when you know more. Calling it off would mean cancelling the trip.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: Your friend asks, “Shall we see the horror film tonight?” You’d prefer the comedy. What do you say?
choices: I’d rather see the comedy. What do you think?
No, horror films are boring. We’re seeing the comedy.
I don’t mind at all. Whatever you’d like to see.
Horror? Seriously? You always pick terrible films.
note: “I’d rather…” gives your preference, and “What do you think?” leaves room for your friend’s. “I don’t mind at all” is the right answer only when you really don’t mind. Here it hides what you want.

picture.alt: A clapperboard beside a film reel.

question: Your friend texts, “I’m at the café by the library. Where are you?” You realise you’ve gone to the café by the station by mistake. What do you reply?
choices: Sorry, wrong café! Stay there, I’m on my way.
You’re in the wrong place. Come to the station café.
Why didn’t you tell me which café you meant?
I’m here now, so I’ll just wait for you to come.
note: The mistake was yours, so you say sorry and you do the walking. “You’re in the wrong place” would be fine if your friend had gone to the wrong café.

question: A friend is booking a table for dinner tonight and asks if you’re coming. You’d like to, but you’ll only find out your work hours at noon. What do you say?
choices: I’d love to come. Can I let you know by twelve?
Yes, definitely! Book me a seat. See you tonight.
Maybe. I’ll see how I feel and text you later.
I don’t know yet. Why do you need to know now?
note: “I’d love to come” shows you want to, and “by twelve” tells your friend when to expect an answer. “Maybe, I’ll see how I feel” sounds as if you’re not very interested.

question: At a concert, your friend wants to stay for the last song. You have to leave now to catch the last ferry home. What do you say?
choices: Sorry, I have to run for my ferry. Enjoy the song!
Come on, we’re leaving now. The ferry won’t wait.
Fine, stay then. I’ll go home on my own, I suppose.
Right, I’m going. See you.
note: You say why you’re leaving, and “Enjoy the song!” lets your friend stay without feeling bad. “Fine, stay then… I suppose” gives the same news but sounds hurt.

picture.alt: A ferry beside an İstanbul skyline.

question: Your friends say, “We’re cycling to the lake, then having lunch there.” Your bike is broken, but there’s a bus to the lake. What do you say?
choices: My bike’s broken, but I can meet you there for lunch.
Sorry, my bike’s broken, so I can’t come. Have a great day.
Can’t you all go by bus instead? Then I can come with you.
Cycling again? Why don’t we ever do anything different?
note: You can’t join the ride, but you can join the lunch, so you say yes to that part. “Can’t you all go by bus?” asks the whole group to change its plan for you.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: On Friday a friend texts, “Tennis next Saturday?” You’re free on both Saturdays, but you’re not sure which one she means. What do you reply?
choices: Sure! Tomorrow, or the Saturday after?
Yes, sure. See you on Saturday!
Which Saturday? You need to be clearer.
“Next Saturday” is confusing. Say the date, please.
note: “Next Saturday” can mean two different days, so naming both clears it up in one friendly question. “See you on Saturday!” sounds nice, but one of you may turn up on the wrong day.

picture.alt: A tennis racket and yellow ball.

question: You’ve planned a picnic in the park with friends today, but it’s pouring with rain. You live nearby. What do you suggest?
choices: How about having the picnic at my flat instead?
We can’t have a picnic in this. It’s cancelled.
Let’s go anyway. A bit of rain never hurt anyone.
You should all come to my place. I’ve decided.
note: “How about…?” suggests a change and lets the others agree to it. “It’s cancelled” and “I’ve decided” make the choice for everyone.

picture.alt: A bowl of salad with croutons.

question: Your friend is having a board game night at her place. A classmate of yours would like to come too. What do you say to your friend?
choices: Would it be OK if I brought someone from my class?
I’ve told my classmate there’s room for one more.
My classmate is coming too, so get an extra chair.
Can I bring a friend? I’m sure you won’t mind.
note: “Would it be OK if…?” lets the host say yes or no. “I’ve told my classmate…” decides for her. It works only if she has already said anyone is welcome.

picture.alt: A wooden game piece beside a die.

question: You and a friend are going to a play. She says, “I’ll buy our tickets online tonight.” You’ve already bought yours. What do you say?
choices: That’s kind, but I’ve already got mine. Just get yours.
Don’t bother, I’ve got mine. You should’ve asked first.
Oh, lovely, thanks! I’ll pay you back for mine.
Why would you buy mine? I can buy my own ticket.
note: “That’s kind, but…” thanks her before the news, and saves her buying a ticket you don’t need. “You should’ve asked first” may be true, but it blames her for a kind offer.

picture.alt: An empty stage framed by red curtains.

question: Your friend missed last Sunday’s photo walk. You’re going again this Sunday and would like her to come. What do you say?
choices: We’re going again on Sunday. Fancy coming this time?
You missed a great walk. You have to come on Sunday.
I don’t suppose you want to come on Sunday, do you?
We’re going on Sunday, if you can be bothered this time.
note: “Fancy coming…?” is a friendly, informal invitation, and “this time” gently refers back to the walk she missed. “I don’t suppose you want to…” sounds as if you expect her to say no.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.
